title: I built a browser off-road racing game with Claude Opus 5.5, Suno, Meshy and ElevenLabs. The ground is simulated and AI trucks dig up the track as they race.
author: Slipfacegame
selftext:
Play it: [https://slipfacegame.com/?utm\_source=reddit&utm\_medium=aigamedev](https://slipfacegame.com/?utm_source=reddit&utm_medium=aigamedev)  
  
Slipface is a free off-road racer that runs in the browser (WebGPU, no download). I’m a solo dev and built it with AI tools:

* **Platform**: browser, desktop. **WebGPU required**: current Chrome or Edge, or Safari 26+ (macOS 26 / iOS 26). Free, no sign-up. Best with PC and gamepad. Also runs on decent mobile (Chrome on Android 12+, Safari on iOS 26+).
* **Code:** Claude Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5. The game, the GPU terrain simulation, the vehicle physics, the AI drivers and the level editor are all written with it.
* **Music:** Suno. Seven tracks, one per kind of level.
* **3D vehicles:** Meshy, from a picture of the car and its tire, then cleaned up and rigged for the physics.
* **Rival voices:** ElevenLabs. Each AI driver has their own voice and callouts.

What the AI did and didn’t do: it wrote most of the code and produced the raw assets, but I decided what the game is, picked and rejected the vehicle pictures, tuned how the trucks drive, and play-tested it.

**The skills that made it repeatable**

The biggest speedup wasn’t a single prompt. It was writing the boring multi-step jobs down once as Claude Code skills, so a repeat is one request and doesn’t need re-explaining:

* **add-vehicle:** takes a brief through Meshy chassis and tire pictures (I approve them), image-to-3D, remeshing to 40k and 10k triangles, compression, the physics preset, the garage entry, rendered tile art and the docs. Sixteen vehicles in, it’s the same checklist every time.
* **add-music:** writes the Suno prompts and then wires the finished tracks in, encoded, mapped to levels and recorded in the docs.
* **compress-assets:** the web build went from about 35 MB to a 13.5 MB first load (15.7 MB on Safari) because every model, texture and track goes through the same pipeline.
* **release:** preflight, commit, push, fast-forward the release branch and verify the live deploy.

The part that took trial and error is that a skill has to say what a human must still approve, like the vehicle pictures, or it will happily generate things you never looked at.

**A level editor, so I’m not stuck with whatever the AI guesses**

Levels are plain JSON, and there’s an in-browser editor that uses the game’s own renderer, terrain simulation and truck. You drag a ridge or a pit into the terrain and drive it seconds later. Every field in the editor is generated from one schema file, so a new brush parameter can’t exist without showing up in the UI.

The game: the terrain is simulated, not painted, so wheels dig real ruts in sand that is still there on the next lap. Up to nine AI rivals race you, and the ruts they dig are the line you have to drive. There’s also a demolition derby, 16 vehicles and leaderboards.

More videos:  [https://www.youtube.com/@Slipface-game](https://www.youtube.com/@Slipface-game)

Happy to answer questions about the workflow: how I prompt for the physics, what Claude got wrong, how I keep AI-generated 3D models small enough for the web.

comments.author: daddywookie
comments.body:
Nice to see an actually walked through process and the results it can bring. A nice antidote to the one shot posts.

It is getting annoying how frequently I have to increase my expectations of what can be created in a browser game. The deformable terrain and atmospheric effects are really good. Is there a large performance impact from these or are they quite simple in execution?

replies.author: Slipfacegame
replies.body:
Thanks, glad the walkthrough was useful. Short answer: the terrain is the expensive-in-principle part, but it’s cheap in practice.

The deformation runs as GPU compute, so the CPU isn’t doing it, and it only simulates the area around the trucks. On my desktop at 1080p the terrain compute pass was around 1 ms and the render pass 1.5–3.7 ms depending on the level. The atmosphere is mostly cheap tricks: the ground mist is a closed-form fog term, and the dust is a few layered draws with no simulation.

I should be upfront that I haven’t properly measured the newest Ultra effects (bloom, depth of field, the blowing-sand layers) yet. The game has four graphics tiers: low, medium, high and ultra. Phones default to medium, and the heavy stuff only turns on at high and ultra, so a weak machine can drop down. If you try it, I’d be curious what GPU you have and which tier is comfortable.

replies.author: Slipfacegame
replies.body: Thanks! There’s 2-player split screen and a ghost of your best lap for now. Online play isn’t planned yet, but I think it could work without matching the terrain exactly on both sides, so I’m thinking about it. No promises on when.

comments.author: MrTheWaffleKing
comments.body: Insanely impressive. I've never seen a browser capable of something like this!

replies.author: Slipfacegame
replies.body: Thank you! A lot of it is WebGPU. Browsers now get real GPU compute shaders, which is what makes ground that deforms possible. Worth trying in a current Chrome, Edge or Safari 26 if you haven’t.

comments.author: titanunveiled
comments.body: Did you have any issues meshy creating “melted” looking textures?

replies.author: Slipfacegame
replies.body:
Yes, some of them, and they still aren’t perfect. Honest answer: the models could be better, and some vehicle took a few rounds. One car I made from a photo of a friend’s Defender, and several of the others started as pictures I generated in ChatGPT.

What I learned about the melted look:

* **The input picture matters most.** If a vehicle looks wrong, I regenerate from a better picture. I don’t try to fix the model. I reject pictures with a tire in the chassis shot, cropped bodies, several vehicles, text or logos, and then pick one of the rest.
* **Never decimate afterwards.** I ask Meshy to remesh to the polygon count I want (40k for the car, 10k for the tire). It re-bakes the texture for the new mesh. Reducing a 300k model afterwards smears the texture into shards, which is what the “melted” look usually is.
* **Glass turns into a checkerboard.** If the picture has a transparent background, glass renders as an opaque checkerboard and Meshy models it. I now describe the windows as empty openings.
* **I look at close-ups of the textures,** not just the mesh, for smeared decals, a seam down the middle of a panel, muddy tires and baked-in shadows.

The rest is still iteration.

replies.author: titanunveiled
replies.body: Thanks for the tips and workflow

comments.author: EnumeratedArray
comments.body:
"The ground remembers" is the most AI sounding thing ever 😂

Really cool demo though, looks great!!

replies.author: Slipfacegame
replies.body:
Ha, fair. 😄 It’s hard to argue with that one. Thanks, glad you like the demo!

True, it is a tagline from an AI. It’s a literal description, though: the ruts really are still there on the next lap. Thanks, glad you like the demo!

replies.author: EnumeratedArray
replies.body: Haha yeah not judging you for it, I just always find it funny when I spot that kinda thing!

replies.author: HuWeiliu
replies.body: I think the problem is that its not a literal description, its weirdly poetic/metaphorical. Needless personification of the ground.

comments.author: Maple-Syrup89
comments.body: Looks great. That sand acceleration is brutal, but perhaps realistic. Love the permanent ruts that actually impact driving on later laps.

replies.author: Slipfacegame
replies.body: Thanks! The sand’s heavy on purpose. When the wheels spin faster than the truck moves, they dig in, and a hole makes it harder to pull out, so a launch with too much throttle buries you. Easing off so the wheels grip is the trick. Tell me if it ever feels unfair rather than hard, since that’s the line I’m trying to get right. Glad you like the ruts!

replies.author: Maple-Syrup89
replies.body: Keep it up, looks pretty great. Do you ever plan to add vehicle damage.

comments.author: Capitinefrobou
comments.body:
Had  blast. Very curious the mechanics and what you did, specially in third track, i noticed the water starting to flood the whole level, i could barely make up the hill... and the water would keep feeling up holes in sand created from tire tracks... thats cool!!

Coincidence, I was working in UE yesterday with a desert map and the chaos vehicles and love what you did here!

replies.author: Slipfacegame
replies.body:
Thanks for playing, and that’s exactly the kind of thing I hoped someone would notice. On Big Climb there’s a spring up on the mesa that keeps adding water for the whole run, and the water is simulated, so it runs downhill and settles in the holes your tires dig. The ruts change where the water goes, and the wet ground then changes how the truck drives, which is why the climb gets harder.

Funny coincidence with the Unreal desert map. Are you using Chaos vehicles for a game or just experimenting? I’d like to hear how it feels there. And if you want details on how any of it works, ask, I’m happy to explain.

replies.author: Capitinefrobou
replies.body:
for a game! i just graduated in game dev and picked up a lot of tools in the past 2 years.... so now i'm building a caravan game, towing vehicles across the desert and other biomes... "sand that remembers " fits it perfectly. here's a clip of where i'm at with the dust and smashable walls. your dust inspired me a lot, the cars stay visible inside it and i'm still chasing that

if you don't mind me asking... does the water change the sand itself, like making it firmer or softer where it runs? and did you ever try letting ruts slowly fill back in over time? thinking about that for places the caravan comes back to later. thanks man, this has been really helpful!!

https://i.redd.it/w8gch956lgvh1.gif

replies.author: Slipfacegame
replies.body:
Congrats on graduating! Caravan game sounds awesome, the tow clip already looks really good. And the dust is nice, you can still see the cars through it. I kept mine pretty faint and low to the ground for that reason.

Yeah, water changes the sand, but in mine wet sand is softer, not firmer. A bit of water makes it less grippy and heavier to drive on, and enough of it turns into mud, which is worse again. Real damp sand can be firmer so its kind of a gameplay choice, but it makes water feel like something to avoid.

Ruts partly fill back in. When sand piles up too steep it slumps down, so deep rut walls collapse a bit, but shallow ones just stay. I havent added any slow refill over time, so cant say how well it would work. For a place the caravan comes back to Id try slowly smoothing the height back to the original when the player is far away. Water also fills the holes like you saw.

Good luck with it, post it when theres more to see!

comments.author: KalElReturns89
comments.body: Seems really cool. Giving me some hope for my Burnout 3 spinoff I'm planning to make sometime soon.

replies.author: Slipfacegame
replies.body: Thanks! A Burnout 3 spinoff sounds awesome, crashes and takedowns are what I’d want to play. If it helps, start small: get one track and one car feeling right before anything else. That’s what worked for me. And post it when you have something to show, I’d like to see it!
